Then they told how they had gone out to hunt seals, and had lost their canoe in the fog, and had struggled back through the water. And they were given more warm water to drink.

They called and called, but no one answered. They were wet and exhausted, and when they had swam across the river they reached the other side, and there in the canoe they sat down and rested.
Then a light came over the water, and they saw a canoe heading toward them. They got in it, and went quickly to the village. They were wet and exhausted, but they were alive. The people of the village gave them warm water to drink, and then they felt better. Then they ate. And after eating they were ready to go out again.

The other man said, "What if something happened to her?" The first man said, "We'd be responsible for her safety." They decided to stay and help her.
After they had waited awhile, the man went to look for her husband. They looked for him all night, and in the morning they found him lying on the ground. The man from Egulac was sorry for the loss, and the woman's husband forgave him. They all went back to the village together. The man from Egulac thought he was going to die for what he had done, but the woman and her husband both knew that he had been trying to help them.
This story is one of several that demonstrate the idea that it is better to err on the side of kindness and help than to hesitate and potentially cause harm. It also shows that true forgiveness works both ways—the woman's husband forgave the errant lover, and the man from Egulac forgave himself.

Origins
"One night two men from Egulac" is a phrase that appears in the early efforts to describe the story, but it is not part of the original. Its origin is uncertain, but it is generally held to be a reference to the location where the story begins, Egulac (Origlada), a town in the province of Piacenza, Italy. The phrase has been interpreted as a pun by L. Sprague De Camp involving the hard g and soft g sounds, a possibility that has been jokingly extended to the pretence that the phrase is a command in a dead language meaning "translate this," with "Egoule" being the Latin term for "tail". The actual etymology is straightforward, involving the Germanic compound eg-wa+lan-t, "estate, fief, province", from Proto-Germanic *гаинवǫ́（nd)) and Latin colonia, a town with Roman legionaries (from Latin colonus, settler). One night two young men from Egulac went down to the river to hunt seals and while they were there it became foggy and calm. Then they heard war-cries, and they thought: "Maybe this is a war-party". But they knew that the sound was too far away for it to be a war-party, and they knew besides that the fog was too thick for arrows to fall good-ly, and they knew that the war-cries were too far away for them to go. But they thought: "Perhaps this is a ghost-party". And they went home again, and in the morning they saw a canoe with two men, and they knew that the ghosts had given them the upper hand. And the two young men from Egulac went down to the river to hunt seals; and they did not see any seals, and they did not see any ghosts, and they returned home again. And the sun rose. It was summer, and they didn't plan to stay out all night, although they did carry blankets. They were young and full of courage, although no match for the grizzly bear. They walked along the river bank, making as little noise as possible, when suddenly a beast, tall as a mountain, rose before them. Its body was covered in hair, and its eyes glowed. One of the young men grabbed his gun and fired at the creature, but without hesitation it knocked both him and his friend into the river. They survived the fall, although they were shivering and exhausted. The bear gave them a wide berth, but made no move to leave. The young men huddled together, cold and frightened, and considered their situation. One of them climbed up the banks and picked up his rifle, which had fallen when he was knocked down. He shot at the bear, narrowly misssing, and his friend started towards the gun. The bear stepped between them, knocked down their guns, and knocked him down again. He dragged him a short distance and then, without further violence, turned and walked quietly away. The other young man, seeing that his friend was safely out of danger, started towards the nearest village. He was cold and exhausted, and could hardly see where he was going. He stumbled over rocks and roots. By dawn he had gained no sense of where he was, and lay down to rest with a rock for a pillow. When he awoke he saw the village ahead of him. He could see smoke rising from the chimneys of the houses, and he knew that he was home. 
There, by the deserted village, two young men sat and waited for the sun to rise. At last they saw a figure descending a path. It came closer and they could see that it was their chief.

First and foremost, it is important to recognize that the passage above is not strictly a narrative in the conventional sense -- it is, rather, a series of events (and descriptions of events) that are conveying information about the culture and cosmology of the Native Americans who inhabited the area. That said, the passage does tell a story, and a rather funny one at that. The two young men make their wish known to the spirits, and in response, they are transformed into balls. The kernels of corn that they discarded at the beginning of the story have been replaced by real corn, which grows overnight and is harvested by the Young Masculine Spirit. The two men then turn back into human form, and in doing so, they leave behind their childish world of make-believe and enter the adult world of hunters and warriors. The story provides a fitting introduction to the more serious themes and beliefs that will follow.

The narrative appears to be a representation of a traditional story from the Ojibwa people, recounted by a Native American storyteller to a white listener. The story appears to embody a number of common themes relating to Native American mythology, including the motif of a trickster figure (in this case the young man who suggests going back to their houses), as well as the theme of transformation, manifested in the metamorphosis of the war-party into birds. The story also touches on the traditional Native American reverence for nature, as seen in the description of the fog and the calmness of the river. Furthermore, the story describes the use of canoes, a staple of Native American transport which was central to their way of life along the rivers and lakes of North America. The narrative also mentions the importance of teamwork and community in Native American culture, as the two men work together to survive the encounter with the war-party.

The legend tells of how the spirit in question came into existence. Some say that it was the ghost of a woman whose body was found around the town of Loc Austin some years previously. Other versions of the legend claim that the spirit was the ghost of a sailor or a soldier who had died somewhere in the general area during the American Revolution and that the spirit became angry when the two men stumbled upon its hiding place and began fishing, thereby disrupting its resting place. Still other versions claim that the spirit was engendered by the death cries of Indians who had been trapped and killed by settlers on the opposite side of the lake, the spirits of which finally bubbled to the surface and emerged as the creature that would later claim the lives of the two fishermen.

The most terrifying aspect of the legend is the prospect of dying at the hands of the vengeful spirit. This spirit, which has come to be known as Skell, has in its repertoire a terrifying array of abilities.

He did not believe them, and they said: "If you do not believe us, let one of us shoot an arrow from his quiver into the other's canoe." One of them shot an arrow, and it was caught by the other, and they counted them again and found that there were four arrows missing. Then the young men said: "We must be dreaming. Let us go back to our village."  (This story is part of a cycle of stories told by the Ojibwa people of North America. The exact meaning of the story is unknown, but it may be a warning against blindly following authority without questioning it.)

"Why not?" asked the stranger. "Because we're not ready. We're too young." The stranger said he thought so too. He had come from the other side of the water and had seen them playing and laughing. In some versions of the story, the two young men walk in the spiritual world at that moment and enter the Dream of the Universe, where they learn important spiritual lessons. Generations later, the grandchildren of the two young men are ready to walk in the spiritual world and learn from the Ancestors.

[/INST] One night, two young Saanich men took a canoe out to the middle of the Strait of Juan de Fuca to talk to the moon. This narrative is often elaborated into a song or a story. It forms the opening of many Indigenous stories of the Pacific Northwest, including those of the Lekws, or Saanich, people, which say that the two men had heard the moon laughing and knew that she was grieving for the loss of her child. The men tried to console her, and in thanking them, the moon gave them the light of the full moon, which they brought back to their people as proof of her gratitude. This myth may be partially responsible for the naming of Vancouver Island by Juan de Fuca, as it was during this voyage that he encountered a group of indigenous people who told him the story of the two young men and the moon.
Canners Island, which is in the straight of Juan de Fuca, is the place where, according to the legend, the two men met the moon, and it is said that the island was pushed up out of the sea by the lunar nymph Nantuck.

One night two young men from Egulac went down to the river for a swim. Their canoe overturned and one of the men was a good swimmer and managed to get to shore, but the other was tired and exhausted and couldn't catch up to the shore before the cold water killed him. 
In an attempt to help his friend, the first man rushed back to the canoe and pushed it out onto the river, but he could swim neither for himself nor for his friend, who was dead now and being swept downstream. The man considered trying to swim to a nearby marshy island, but the current was strong and he couldn't make it that far. Instead, he struck out for the opposite shore, vowing to call for help when he reached it. After an exhausting and frightening ordeal, he finally made it to the other side, almost fainting from exhaustion. 
In the meantime, the villagers on the far side had seen the two men leave for a swim for long enough that they had gone to look for them. Upon finding the canoe overturned and empty, they had gone to the shore where the first man was now gasping for air. He reported that his friend had been swept downstream and was surely gone for good.
The villagers had heard rumors of a deadly current in the middle of the river, but never believed them - besides, the rumored current would be illegal to swim in, since it is called Cholo that has claimed many lives. The villagers had always believed it to be a myth. Now they weren't so sure.

One of the young men turned around and was shot and killed by the farmer. The other young man ran home to Egulac and reported the death to his family and the rest of the Cree people. The farmer was arrested and brought to trial, but justice had already been served in another manner. The entire Cree population had gathered at the spot where the young man had been killed. A group of them stole away to the farmer's village and burned down his house and killed his cattle. Then they stole all of his crops and took them back to Egulac. No otherWhite settler dared enter the Cree village after that night.

A few moments later, however, their friends appeared along the bank of the river, and after exchanging cheerful greetings, the two groups of men sat down together and began to feast upon the fish that they had caught.
As they sat there, smoking their pipes of sage and watching the bubbles rise in the water near their canoes, it occurred to the two young men that it was indeed a very good thing that they had come down to the river that day. For although they had not gone out searching for their fellow hunters, their friends must have been in trouble and had called for their aid. Now, as they all sat together and enjoyed their meal, everything was quiet and peaceful.
But suddenly, from the depths of the water there came a loud thud, and the ground beneath them began to tremble. At first the men looked at one another in surprise, but then they noticed that the bubbles in the water had stopped bubbling, and a terrible blackness came sweeping toward them across the face of the water. And so, in a great rush of water and darkness, the two men were taken down beneath the surface of the river.

Before long, the conversation turned to things of a more substantive nature, and Er:lu revealed that he was running away from something. Bazil insisted that he tell them everything, but the stranger refused and begged them not to lead him back to his home village lest he be killed for running away.
